Each problem below is mapped to the data finding, the dashboard visual that surfaces it, and the executive decision it enables. The goal is to make every chart on the dashboard defensible: if an executive asks \"why does this chart exist?\", the answer is one of the six problems below.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch3 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eProblem 1 — Geographic Revenue Concentration Risk\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-problem-1--geographic-revenue-concentration-risk\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: Problem 1 — Geographic Revenue Concentration Risk\" href=\"#problem-1--geographic-revenue-concentration-risk\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eThe question a VP of Commercial would ask:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cblockquote\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\"If São Paulo sneezes, do we catch a cold? How much of our revenue depends on a single state?\"\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/blockquote\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat the data shows:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eSão Paulo (SP) alone drives \u003cstrong\u003eR$5.77M (37%)\u003c/strong\u003e of total revenue with 40,501 orders. The top three states — SP, RJ, MG — together generate \u003cstrong\u003eR$9.64M (63%)\u003c/strong\u003e of revenue. The remaining 24 states share only 37% of the business. This is a textbook single-market dependency: a regulatory change, a regional logistics disruption, or a competitor push in the Southeast could materially impact the entire P\u0026amp;L. At the same time, the average order value in underpenetrated states like BA (R$160) is \u003cstrong\u003e29% higher\u003c/strong\u003e than in SP (R$124) — meaning the markets Olist has not yet captured are, per order, more valuable than the market it dominates.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHow the dashboard answers it:\u003c/strong\u003e The \"Top 10 States by Revenue\" bar chart on Page 1, with enriched tooltips showing revenue, order count, average delivery days, and average order value per state in a single hover. An executive can scan the chart in 5 seconds and immediately see both the concentration and the per-order upside of expansion markets.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eRecommended Action\u003c/strong\u003e Treat SP as the home market requiring depth (faster delivery, wider assortment, in-region warehousing). Launch a premium-category pilot in BA — small population, 29% higher AOV than SP, low current penetration. This is a low-risk expansion bet that the concentration metric alone would not surface.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch3 tabindex=\"-1\" ask:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cblockquote\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\"Which categories are carrying the business, and how exposed are we if one of them drops?\"\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/blockquote\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat the data shows:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThe top 10 categories generate \u003cstrong\u003eR$9.53M (62%)\u003c/strong\u003e of revenue. \u003ccode\u003ehealth_beauty\u003c/code\u003e (R$1.41M, 9,465 orders), \u003ccode\u003ewatches_gifts\u003c/code\u003e (R$1.26M, 5,859 orders), and \u003ccode\u003ebed_bath_table\u003c/code\u003e (R$1.23M, 10,953 orders) are the three pillars. Notably, \u003ccode\u003ewatches_gifts\u003c/code\u003e delivers near-equivalent revenue to \u003ccode\u003ebed_bath_table\u003c/code\u003e with \u003cstrong\u003ehalf the order volume\u003c/strong\u003e — it is a high-AOV category that punches above its weight. Losing a single top seller in \u003ccode\u003ewatches_gifts\u003c/code\u003e could cost more revenue than a five-category drop in \u003ccode\u003ehousewares\u003c/code\u003e. This asymmetry is invisible if you only look at revenue; it only becomes apparent when you compare revenue per order across categories, which is exactly what the dashboard's Revenue/Orders toggle is designed to expose.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHow the dashboard answers it:\u003c/strong\u003e The dynamic \"Top 10 Categories\" bar chart on Page 2 — users toggle between Revenue and Orders via a slicer (disconnected-table pattern with DAX \u003ccode\u003eSWITCH\u003c/code\u003e + \u003ccode\u003eSELECTEDVALUE\u003c/code\u003e). Flipping between the two views reveals which categories are volume drivers (e.g., \u003ccode\u003ebed_bath_table\u003c/code\u003e — many orders, moderate revenue) vs. value drivers (e.g., \u003ccode\u003ewatches_gifts\u003c/code\u003e — fewer orders, high revenue).\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eRecommended Action:\u003c/strong\u003e  Protect watches_gifts aggressively — exclusive seller partnerships, expanded assortment, proactive stock verification. Losing one top watches seller would cost more revenue than losing three average sellers in housewares. This is also the highest-ROI category for a seller-loyalty program (preferred fees, priority placement).\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch3 ask:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cblockquote\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\"Which categories are consistently breaching our delivery promise, and why?\"\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/blockquote\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat the data shows:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThe catalog-wide average delivery time is around \u003cstrong\u003e12 days\u003c/strong\u003e, but several categories massively overshoot: \u003ccode\u003eoffice_furniture\u003c/code\u003e at \u003cstrong\u003e20.8 days\u003c/strong\u003e (73% above average), \u003ccode\u003echristmas_supplies\u003c/code\u003e (15.7), \u003ccode\u003efashion_shoes\u003c/code\u003e (15.4), \u003ccode\u003efurniture_mattress_and_upholstery\u003c/code\u003e (14.4), and \u003ccode\u003ehome_appliances_2\u003c/code\u003e (13.9). The pattern is clear and physical: \u003cstrong\u003ebulky, heavy, or oversized items\u003c/strong\u003e take 50–70% longer to deliver than the platform average. By contrast, fast-moving consumables like \u003ccode\u003efood\u003c/code\u003e (9.6 days) and \u003ccode\u003eparty_supplies\u003c/code\u003e (9.3) deliver well under the average. A buyer who orders a mattress and a party decoration in the same week receives the party supplies in 9 days and waits another 5 days for the mattress — and blames Olist, not the seller.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHow the dashboard answers it:\u003c/strong\u003e The \"Avg Delivery Time by Category\" chart on Page 2 — sorted descending so the worst performers surface at the top immediately. The visual makes the bulky-category pattern impossible to miss.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eRecommended Action:\u003c/strong\u003e Introduce category-specific delivery promises at checkout (e.g., \"12–18 business days for furniture\") so buyer expectations match operational reality. In parallel, negotiate a dedicated bulky-freight contract with a national carrier — the bottleneck is physical (heavy/oversized items require scheduled freight), not seller laziness.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch3 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eProblem 4 — Cancellation Risk in Niche Categories\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-problem-4--cancellation-risk-in-niche-categories\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: Problem 4 — Cancellation Risk in Niche Categories\" href=\"#problem-4--cancellation-risk-in-niche-categories\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eThe question a Head of Seller Quality would ask:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cblockquote\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\"Which categories have a cancellation problem that is eroding buyer trust?\"\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/blockquote\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat the data shows:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003ePlatform-wide cancellation rate is \u003cstrong\u003e0.63%\u003c/strong\u003e — healthy by e-commerce standards. But several niche categories significantly overshoot: \u003ccode\u003eportateis_cozinha_e_preparadores_de_alimentos\u003c/code\u003e at \u003cstrong\u003e6.67%\u003c/strong\u003e (small sample but flagrant), \u003ccode\u003edvds_blu_ray\u003c/code\u003e (3.13%), \u003ccode\u003econstruction_tools_safety\u003c/code\u003e (\u003cstrong\u003e2.58%\u003c/strong\u003e with 194 orders — meaningful volume), and \u003ccode\u003ediapers_and_hygiene\u003c/code\u003e (2.56%). \u003ccode\u003emusical_instruments\u003c/code\u003e (1.62% on 680 orders) is also worth attention because of its scale. A 2.5%+ cancellation rate at meaningful volume signals either seller-side stock issues (overselling inventory they don't have) or product-quality disputes (buyers rejecting goods on delivery). Either way, every canceled order is a customer who will think twice before buying from Olist again.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHow the dashboard answers it:\u003c/strong\u003e The \"Cancellation Rate by Category\" bonus chart on Page 2 — filtered with \u003ccode\u003eHAVING COUNT(*) \u0026gt; 10\u003c/code\u003e to exclude statistically noisy micro-categories where 1 cancellation in 3 orders would otherwise show a misleading 33% rate.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eRecommended Action\u003c/strong\u003e Trigger seller audits in construction_tools_safety (2.58% on 194 orders) and musical_instruments (1.62% on 680 orders) — these have meaningful volume, not statistical noise. Require inventory verification before listing for any seller exceeding 2% cancellation rate. Cap daily order acceptance for chronic offenders pending remediation.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch3 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eProblem 5 — Customer Retention Crisis\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-problem-5--customer-retention-crisis\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: Problem 5 — Customer Retention Crisis\" href=\"#problem-5--customer-retention-crisis\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eThe question a Head of CRM / Growth would ask:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cblockquote\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\"Are we a one-purchase marketplace? Why don't customers come back?\"\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/blockquote\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat the data shows:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eOnly \u003cstrong\u003e2,801 of 93,358 customers (3.0%)\u003c/strong\u003e have ever placed a second order. Repeat customers contribute just \u003cstrong\u003e5.6%\u003c/strong\u003e of total revenue (R$864K of R$15.4M). Segmenting by lifetime spend reveals an even starker picture: \u003cstrong\u003e95.4%\u003c/strong\u003e of customers fall into the Low segment (\u0026lt;500 BRL lifetime), contributing 74.5% of revenue. The Premium segment (\u0026gt;1,000 BRL) is just \u003cstrong\u003e1.2%\u003c/strong\u003e of the base (1,148 customers) but drives \u003cstrong\u003e11.8%\u003c/strong\u003e of revenue. Olist is, in effect, running a one-shot acquisition engine — every new customer must be won from scratch because almost none return. The arithmetic is brutal: acquiring a new customer in Brazil costs roughly R$30–60 in paid media, but with a 3% repeat rate, the lifetime revenue per acquired customer barely clears that cost.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHow the dashboard answers it:\u003c/strong\u003e The \"Repeat Customer Rate\" KPI card on Page 1 (with revenue contribution shown alongside), plus the \"Revenue by Customer Segment\" bar chart with self-explanatory subtitle (Low \u0026lt;500 | Regular 500–1000 | Premium \u0026gt;1000 BRL). The segment subtitle is critical: without it, an executive would have to ask what \"Low\" means, breaking the self-service principle.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eRecommended Action:\u003c/strong\u003e  Launch a post-purchase lifecycle program: day-7 review prompt → day-30 category re-engagement → day-90 loyalty offer. Prioritize the Premium segment (1,148 customers, R$1.8M revenue) for early experiments. The math: even a 1-point lift in repeat rate (3% → 4%) unlocks ~R$1.5M of incremental revenue from the existing 93K customer base, with zero acquisition spend.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003cdiv ask:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cblockquote\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\"When do we need to surge inventory, staffing, and logistics capacity — and by how much?\"\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/blockquote\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhat the data shows:\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eMonthly revenue grew from \u003cstrong\u003eR$143K (Sep 2016)\u003c/strong\u003e to \u003cstrong\u003eR$1.13M (Apr 2018)\u003c/strong\u003e — an 8x expansion in 19 months. But the most striking signal is \u003cstrong\u003eNovember 2017\u003c/strong\u003e: revenue jumped to \u003cstrong\u003eR$1.15M with 7,289 orders\u003c/strong\u003e, a \u003cstrong\u003e53% month-over-month spike\u003c/strong\u003e from October's R$751K, then dropped back to R$843K in December. This is unambiguously a Black Friday effect, and it means Olist's logistics, customer support, and seller operations must be sized to absorb a ~50% demand surge in a single month — every year. The same pattern likely repeats in November 2018 (data ends in August 2018, so this cannot be confirmed from the dataset, but the structural signal is clear).\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHow the dashboard answers it:\u003c/strong\u003e The \"Monthly Revenue Trend\" line chart on Page 1, with order count and unique customer count also available in the underlying data for capacity planning. The November spike is visually unmissable on the line chart.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eRecommended Action\u003c/strong\u003e  Pre-position inventory in SP warehouses by October 15. Surge customer-support headcount by November 1. Lock in seller-side stock commitments 60 days in advance. Open a temporary logistics-provider contract for the November 15–30 window. Under-provisioning for November is the most expensive operational mistake Olist can make — every canceled order during the peak window compounds Problem 5.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003chr\u003e\n\u003cdiv <p dir="auto">This project analyzes ~99,000 orders from the Olist Brazilian e-commerce marketplace (2016–2018) and surfaces actionable insights for executives through a <strong>2-page Power BI dashboard</strong>.</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li><strong>Page 1 — Executive Overview</strong>: Revenue trend, customer segmentation, top states</li>
<li><strong>Page 2 — Sales & Product Analysis</strong>: Category performance, delivery times, weekend vs weekday behavior</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The project was built as part of a SQL end-to-end bootcamp and enhanced with intermediate-to-advanced Power BI patterns (DAX, disconnected tables, dynamic measures, enriched tooltips).</p>
<hr>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h2 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">🎯 Business Problems Solved</h2><a id="user-content--business-problems-solved" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 🎯 Business Problems Solved" href="#-business-problems-solved"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">This dashboard is not a technical showcase — it answers six concrete business questions that Olist's commercial and operations leadership face every quarter. Each problem below is mapped to the data finding, the dashboard visual that surfaces it, and the executive decision it enables. The goal is to make every chart on the dashboard defensible: if an executive asks "why does this chart exist?", the answer is one of the six problems below.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Problem 1 — Geographic Revenue Concentration Risk</h3><a id="user-content-problem-1--geographic-revenue-concentration-risk" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Problem 1 — Geographic Revenue Concentration Risk" href="#problem-1--geographic-revenue-concentration-risk"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto"><strong>The question a VP of Commercial would ask:</strong></p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">"If São Paulo sneezes, do we catch a cold? How much of our revenue depends on a single state?"</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto"><strong>What the data shows:</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">São Paulo (SP) alone drives <strong>R$5.77M (37%)</strong> of total revenue with 40,501 orders. The top three states — SP, RJ, MG — together generate <strong>R$9.64M (63%)</strong> of revenue. The remaining 24 states share only 37% of the business. This is a textbook single-market dependency: a regulatory change, a regional logistics disruption, or a competitor push in the Southeast could materially impact the entire P&L. At the same time, the average order value in underpenetrated states like BA (R$160) is <strong>29% higher</strong> than in SP (R$124) — meaning the markets Olist has not yet captured are, per order, more valuable than the market it dominates.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>How the dashboard answers it:</strong> The "Top 10 States by Revenue" bar chart on Page 1, with enriched tooltips showing revenue, order count, average delivery days, and average order value per state in a single hover. An executive can scan the chart in 5 seconds and immediately see both the concentration and the per-order upside of expansion markets.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Recommended Action</strong> Treat SP as the home market requiring depth (faster delivery, wider assortment, in-region warehousing). Launch a premium-category pilot in BA — small population, 29% higher AOV than SP, low current penetration. This is a low-risk expansion bet that the concentration metric alone would not surface.</p>
<hr>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Problem 2 — Category Portfolio Dependency</h3><a id="user-content-problem-2--category-portfolio-dependency" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Problem 2 — Category Portfolio Dependency" href="#problem-2--category-portfolio-dependency"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto"><strong>The question a Category Manager would ask:</strong></p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">"Which categories are carrying the business, and how exposed are we if one of them drops?"</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto"><strong>What the data shows:</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">The top 10 categories generate <strong>R$9.53M (62%)</strong> of revenue. <code>health_beauty</code> (R$1.41M, 9,465 orders), <code>watches_gifts</code> (R$1.26M, 5,859 orders), and <code>bed_bath_table</code> (R$1.23M, 10,953 orders) are the three pillars. Notably, <code>watches_gifts</code> delivers near-equivalent revenue to <code>bed_bath_table</code> with <strong>half the order volume</strong> — it is a high-AOV category that punches above its weight. Losing a single top seller in <code>watches_gifts</code> could cost more revenue than a five-category drop in <code>housewares</code>. This asymmetry is invisible if you only look at revenue; it only becomes apparent when you compare revenue per order across categories, which is exactly what the dashboard's Revenue/Orders toggle is designed to expose.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>How the dashboard answers it:</strong> The dynamic "Top 10 Categories" bar chart on Page 2 — users toggle between Revenue and Orders via a slicer (disconnected-table pattern with DAX <code>SWITCH</code> + <code>SELECTEDVALUE</code>). Flipping between the two views reveals which categories are volume drivers (e.g., <code>bed_bath_table</code> — many orders, moderate revenue) vs. value drivers (e.g., <code>watches_gifts</code> — fewer orders, high revenue).</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Recommended Action:</strong>  Protect watches_gifts aggressively — exclusive seller partnerships, expanded assortment, proactive stock verification. Losing one top watches seller would cost more revenue than losing three average sellers in housewares. This is also the highest-ROI category for a seller-loyalty program (preferred fees, priority placement).</p>
<hr>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Problem 3 — Delivery Time SLA Breaches in Bulky Categories</h3><a id="user-content-problem-3--delivery-time-sla-breaches-in-bulky-categories" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Problem 3 — Delivery Time SLA Breaches in Bulky Categories" href="#problem-3--delivery-time-sla-breaches-in-bulky-categories"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto"><strong>The question a Head of Operations would ask:</strong></p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">"Which categories are consistently breaching our delivery promise, and why?"</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto"><strong>What the data shows:</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">The catalog-wide average delivery time is around <strong>12 days</strong>, but several categories massively overshoot: <code>office_furniture</code> at <strong>20.8 days</strong> (73% above average), <code>christmas_supplies</code> (15.7), <code>fashion_shoes</code> (15.4), <code>furniture_mattress_and_upholstery</code> (14.4), and <code>home_appliances_2</code> (13.9). The pattern is clear and physical: <strong>bulky, heavy, or oversized items</strong> take 50–70% longer to deliver than the platform average. By contrast, fast-moving consumables like <code>food</code> (9.6 days) and <code>party_supplies</code> (9.3) deliver well under the average. A buyer who orders a mattress and a party decoration in the same week receives the party supplies in 9 days and waits another 5 days for the mattress — and blames Olist, not the seller.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>How the dashboard answers it:</strong> The "Avg Delivery Time by Category" chart on Page 2 — sorted descending so the worst performers surface at the top immediately. The visual makes the bulky-category pattern impossible to miss.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Recommended Action:</strong> Introduce category-specific delivery promises at checkout (e.g., "12–18 business days for furniture") so buyer expectations match operational reality. In parallel, negotiate a dedicated bulky-freight contract with a national carrier — the bottleneck is physical (heavy/oversized items require scheduled freight), not seller laziness.</p>
<hr>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Problem 4 — Cancellation Risk in Niche Categories</h3><a id="user-content-problem-4--cancellation-risk-in-niche-categories" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Problem 4 — Cancellation Risk in Niche Categories" href="#problem-4--cancellation-risk-in-niche-categories"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto"><strong>The question a Head of Seller Quality would ask:</strong></p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">"Which categories have a cancellation problem that is eroding buyer trust?"</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto"><strong>What the data shows:</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">Platform-wide cancellation rate is <strong>0.63%</strong> — healthy by e-commerce standards. But several niche categories significantly overshoot: <code>portateis_cozinha_e_preparadores_de_alimentos</code> at <strong>6.67%</strong> (small sample but flagrant), <code>dvds_blu_ray</code> (3.13%), <code>construction_tools_safety</code> (<strong>2.58%</strong> with 194 orders — meaningful volume), and <code>diapers_and_hygiene</code> (2.56%). <code>musical_instruments</code> (1.62% on 680 orders) is also worth attention because of its scale. A 2.5%+ cancellation rate at meaningful volume signals either seller-side stock issues (overselling inventory they don't have) or product-quality disputes (buyers rejecting goods on delivery). Either way, every canceled order is a customer who will think twice before buying from Olist again.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>How the dashboard answers it:</strong> The "Cancellation Rate by Category" bonus chart on Page 2 — filtered with <code>HAVING COUNT(*) > 10</code> to exclude statistically noisy micro-categories where 1 cancellation in 3 orders would otherwise show a misleading 33% rate.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Recommended Action</strong> Trigger seller audits in construction_tools_safety (2.58% on 194 orders) and musical_instruments (1.62% on 680 orders) — these have meaningful volume, not statistical noise. Require inventory verification before listing for any seller exceeding 2% cancellation rate. Cap daily order acceptance for chronic offenders pending remediation.</p>
<hr>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Problem 5 — Customer Retention Crisis</h3><a id="user-content-problem-5--customer-retention-crisis" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Problem 5 — Customer Retention Crisis" href="#problem-5--customer-retention-crisis"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto"><strong>The question a Head of CRM / Growth would ask:</strong></p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">"Are we a one-purchase marketplace? Why don't customers come back?"</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto"><strong>What the data shows:</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">Only <strong>2,801 of 93,358 customers (3.0%)</strong> have ever placed a second order. Repeat customers contribute just <strong>5.6%</strong> of total revenue (R$864K of R$15.4M). Segmenting by lifetime spend reveals an even starker picture: <strong>95.4%</strong> of customers fall into the Low segment (<500 BRL lifetime), contributing 74.5% of revenue. The Premium segment (>1,000 BRL) is just <strong>1.2%</strong> of the base (1,148 customers) but drives <strong>11.8%</strong> of revenue. Olist is, in effect, running a one-shot acquisition engine — every new customer must be won from scratch because almost none return. The arithmetic is brutal: acquiring a new customer in Brazil costs roughly R$30–60 in paid media, but with a 3% repeat rate, the lifetime revenue per acquired customer barely clears that cost.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>How the dashboard answers it:</strong> The "Repeat Customer Rate" KPI card on Page 1 (with revenue contribution shown alongside), plus the "Revenue by Customer Segment" bar chart with self-explanatory subtitle (Low <500 | Regular 500–1000 | Premium >1000 BRL). The segment subtitle is critical: without it, an executive would have to ask what "Low" means, breaking the self-service principle.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Recommended Action:</strong>  Launch a post-purchase lifecycle program: day-7 review prompt → day-30 category re-engagement → day-90 loyalty offer. Prioritize the Premium segment (1,148 customers, R$1.8M revenue) for early experiments. The math: even a 1-point lift in repeat rate (3% → 4%) unlocks ~R$1.5M of incremental revenue from the existing 93K customer base, with zero acquisition spend.</p>
<hr>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Problem 6 — Seasonal Capacity Planning (Black Friday Spike)</h3><a id="user-content-problem-6--seasonal-capacity-planning-black-friday-spike" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Problem 6 — Seasonal Capacity Planning (Black Friday Spike)" href="#problem-6--seasonal-capacity-planning-black-friday-spike"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto"><strong>The question a Head of Supply Chain would ask:</strong></p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">"When do we need to surge inventory, staffing, and logistics capacity — and by how much?"</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto"><strong>What the data shows:</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">Monthly revenue grew from <strong>R$143K (Sep 2016)</strong> to <strong>R$1.13M (Apr 2018)</strong> — an 8x expansion in 19 months. But the most striking signal is <strong>November 2017</strong>: revenue jumped to <strong>R$1.15M with 7,289 orders</strong>, a <strong>53% month-over-month spike</strong> from October's R$751K, then dropped back to R$843K in December. This is unambiguously a Black Friday effect, and it means Olist's logistics, customer support, and seller operations must be sized to absorb a ~50% demand surge in a single month — every year. The same pattern likely repeats in November 2018 (data ends in August 2018, so this cannot be confirmed from the dataset, but the structural signal is clear).</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>How the dashboard answers it:</strong> The "Monthly Revenue Trend" line chart on Page 1, with order count and unique customer count also available in the underlying data for capacity planning. The November spike is visually unmissable on the line chart.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Recommended Action</strong>  Pre-position inventory in SP warehouses by October 15. Surge customer-support headcount by November 1. Lock in seller-side stock commitments 60 days in advance. Open a temporary logistics-provider contract for the November 15–30 window. Under-provisioning for November is the most expensive operational mistake Olist can make — every canceled order during the peak window compounds Problem 5.</p>

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">1. Data accuracy fix — Cancellation Rate KPI</h3><a id="user-content-1-data-accuracy-fix--cancellation-rate-kpi" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 1. Data accuracy fix — Cancellation Rate KPI" href="#1-data-accuracy-fix--cancellation-rate-kpi"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">The original Global KPIs query used <code>WHERE order_status != 'canceled'</code> to compute revenue from realized orders. This filter silently broke the cancellation-rate calculation (it returned <code>0.0%</code> because canceled rows were filtered out before being counted).</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Fix</strong>: Split into two separate queries — one for revenue (with filter), one for cancellation rate (without filter). Data accuracy > convenience.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">2. Disconnected table pattern for dynamic metrics</h3><a id="user-content-2-disconnected-table-pattern-for-dynamic-metrics" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 2. Disconnected table pattern for dynamic metrics" href="#2-disconnected-table-pattern-for-dynamic-metrics"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">Instead of building two separate bar charts for "Top 10 Categories by Revenue" and "Top 10 Categories by Orders", I used a <strong>disconnected table</strong> (<code>MetricSelector</code>) + a DAX <code>SWITCH</code> measure (<code>SelectedMetricValue</code>) + a slicer. The chart title is also dynamic via <strong>Field Value formatting</strong> (<code>SelectedMetricTitle</code>).</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">3. Enriched tooltips — context over single metrics</h3><a id="user-content-3-enriched-tooltips--context-over-single-metrics" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3. Enriched tooltips — context over single metrics" href="#3-enriched-tooltips--context-over-single-metrics"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">The Top 10 States chart shows not only revenue but also total orders, avg delivery days, and avg order value in its tooltip. Following Microsoft/Amazon executive-reporting principles: a single metric is half-analysis — context is what enables decisions.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">4. SQL readability — COALESCE for category translation</h3><a id="user-content-4-sql-readability--coalesce-for-category-translation" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 4. SQL readability — COALESCE for category translation" href="#4-sql-readability--coalesce-for-category-translation"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">Category names are stored in Portuguese. A <code>LEFT JOIN</code> to <code>product_category_name_translation</code> combined with <code>COALESCE</code> lets the dashboard prefer English names but gracefully fall back to Portuguese when a translation is missing.</p>
